lead: An aperture antenna radiates from an opening, not from a thin wire: the field spread across the opening sets the beam, and the wider the opening in wavelengths, the narrower the beam. A horn is the commonest aperture: a waveguide whose walls flare out so that the guided wave grows gently to a large opening instead of meeting free space at an abrupt end. Babinet’s principle links a slot cut in a metal sheet to a metal strip of the same shape, so the slot antennas on aircraft skins and waveguide walls can be worked out from dipole results.
prereq: You need: the TE<sub>10</sub> mode of rectangular waveguide from the waveguide topic, and directivity, gain and effective aperture from the antenna fundamentals topic.

blocks.text: Across the opening the field has an amplitude and a phase at every point; this aperture field is the source of the far field. A field of equal amplitude and phase everywhere (uniform illumination) gives the narrowest beam for the size but high sidelobes. A field that falls toward the edges (a taper) lowers the sidelobes and widens the beam, just as the amplitude tapers of arrays do. A phase that varies across the opening spoils the beam further.

blocks.where: A<sub>e</sub> is the effective aperture in m²; A is the physical area of the opening in m²; η<sub>ap</sub> is the aperture efficiency (0 to 1), which counts taper and phase error.

D is the directivity as a ratio; λ is the free-space wavelength in m. For a horn with negligible wall loss the gain G equals D; with loss, G = e<sub>r</sub>D, where e<sub>r</sub> is the radiation efficiency.

blocks.text: A rectangular waveguide fed in the TE<sub>10</sub> mode already has a cosine taper across its broad wall, so even a perfect horn opening has η<sub>ap</sub> ≈ 0.81 from taper alone; the phase error of a practical flare brings it down to about 0.5. Aperture efficiency is not radiation efficiency: one is about how well the opening is used, the other about power lost as heat.

Flaring only the walls in the plane of the electric field (the narrow walls of the TE10 guide) gives an E-plane sectoral horn; flaring only the broad walls, in the plane of the magnetic field, gives an H-plane sectoral horn; flaring both gives the pyramidal horn, the usual gain standard. A conical horn flares a circular guide; a corrugated horn has rings cut inside, which give equal E- and H-plane patterns and low cross-polarization for reflector feeds.

The wave inside the flare spreads from the apex as a cylindrical or spherical front, so it reaches the edge of the opening later than the centre. For an opening of width a and a length ℓ from the apex, the extra path at the edge is about δ = a²/(8ℓ). A short horn with a wide flare has a large δ, which fills the nulls, raises the sidelobes and lowers the gain. The optimum horn gives the most gain for its length; it allows δ = 0.25λ in the E-plane and δ = 0.375λ in the H-plane (the H-plane can take more because the cosine taper already weakens the edges):

A is the H-plane width and B the E-plane height of the opening; ℓ<sub>E</sub> and ℓ<sub>H</sub> are the apex-to-aperture lengths for optimum flares. An optimum pyramidal horn has η<sub>ap</sub> ≈ 0.5.
Half-power beamwidths in degrees of an optimum horn. The H-plane beam is wider for the same size because of the cosine taper.

Babinet’s principle in optics says that the fields behind a screen with a hole and behind the complementary screen (a flat piece the shape of the hole) add up to the field with no screen at all. Booker extended it to electromagnetic waves: the complementary screen must also swap the electric and magnetic fields, so the sum is a vector sum with the polarization turned through 90°.

The useful result: a narrow slot cut in a large conducting sheet radiates the same pattern as a dipole of the same length and shape, with E and H interchanged. A horizontal slot therefore radiates like a vertical dipole. The pattern is shared, but the impedance is not:

η<sub>0</sub> = 120π ≈ 377 Ω is the impedance of free space, so η<sub>0</sub>²/4 ≈ 35 530 Ω². Z<sub>slot</sub> and Z<sub>dipole</sub> are the input impedances of the slot and its complementary strip dipole.

Since a dipole is a low-impedance antenna, its complementary slot is a high-impedance one, and a dipole that is inductive gives a slot that is capacitive. Slots are flush with the surface, so they suit aircraft and missiles; rows of slots cut in a waveguide wall make the slotted-waveguide arrays of marine radars.

examples.question: A pyramidal horn at 10 GHz has an opening A = 10 cm (H-plane) by B = 8 cm (E-plane) and aperture efficiency 0.5. Find the gain in dBi, the two half-power beamwidths, and the apex lengths that make both flares optimum.
steps: Optimum E-plane length: ℓ<sub>E</sub> = B²/(2λ) = 64/6 = 10.7 cm. Check δ = B²/(8ℓ<sub>E</sub>) = 64/85.3 = 0.75 cm = 0.25λ.
Optimum H-plane length: ℓ<sub>H</sub> = A²/(3λ) = 100/9 = 11.1 cm. Check δ = 100/(8 × 11.1) = 1.125 cm = 0.375λ.
Unit check: the area went into the formula in m² and λ² in m², so the ratio has no unit.
examples.answer: G = 55.9, that is 17.5 dBi; beamwidths about 21.0° (E-plane) and 20.1° (H-plane); apex lengths about 10.7 cm (E) and 11.1 cm (H) for optimum flares. The near-square beam comes from the larger H-plane width offsetting its taper.

examples.question: A half-wave strip dipole has Z = 73 + j42.5 Ω. Find the input impedance of the complementary half-wave slot, and the slot resistance when the strip is trimmed to resonance at 73 Ω. How long is the slot at 10 GHz?
steps: At resonance: Z<sub>slot</sub> = 35 530/73 = 487 Ω, purely resistive.
The inductive dipole (+j42.5) gave a capacitive slot (−j212), as the Booker relation predicts.
Length at 10 GHz: λ/2 = 3 cm/2 = 1.5 cm.
examples.answer: Z<sub>slot</sub> ≈ 363 − j212 Ω for the half-wave slot and about 487 Ω at resonance; the slot is about 1.5 cm long at 10 GHz. Such a high resistance is why slots are fed off-centre or from a waveguide rather than straight from a 50 Ω cable.

traps: Using the physical area in D = 4πA/λ². Use A<sub>e</sub> = η<sub>ap</sub>A; with A the 10 × 8 cm horn would come out at 111.7 (20.5 dBi), 3 dB too high.
Converting cm² to m² wrongly. 80 cm² is 0.0080 m², not 0.80 m².
Thinking a wider flare always means more gain. For a fixed length, a wider opening brings a larger phase error δ and past the optimum the gain falls.
Giving the slot the dipole’s impedance. Only the pattern carries over; the impedance follows Z<sub>slot</sub>Z<sub>dipole</sub> = η<sub>0</sub>²/4, and the polarization turns through 90°.
Calling aperture efficiency radiation efficiency. η<sub>ap</sub> is about illumination and phase; e<sub>r</sub> is about heat loss.

quiz.a: η<sub>ap</sub> = A<sub>e</sub>/A, the effective aperture over the physical area; it accounts for amplitude taper and phase error.

quiz.q: Name the three kinds of rectangular horn and the walls each flares.
quiz.a: E-plane sectoral (narrow walls, in the E-field plane), H-plane sectoral (broad walls, in the H-field plane), pyramidal (both).

quiz.q: Why does a short horn with a wide flare have low gain?
quiz.a: The wave reaches the edges of the opening later than the centre by δ = a²/(8ℓ); a large δ means the aperture is far from in phase, so the main beam broadens, nulls fill and gain drops.

quiz.q: A 20 cm × 10 cm aperture at 5 GHz has η<sub>ap</sub> = 0.6. Find A<sub>e</sub> and the gain in dBi.
Find the optimum H-plane length for a 12 cm wide opening at 6 GHz.
A slot and its complementary dipole have the same pattern. Why not the same impedance or polarization?
quiz.a: Booker’s form of Babinet’s principle swaps E and H between the two screens: the slot acts as a magnetic current where the dipole is an electric current. The pattern shape is shared, the polarization turns 90°, and the impedances obey Z<sub>slot</sub>Z<sub>dipole</sub> = η<sub>0</sub>²/4.

quiz.q: A horn is shortened by widening its flare angle while keeping the opening size. What happens to gain and pattern?
quiz.a: ℓ falls, so δ = a²/(8ℓ) grows; once δ passes the optimum (0.25λ E-plane, 0.375λ H-plane) the gain falls, the beam broadens and the sidelobes rise.

beyond: Not for the exam. Horn designs are now checked with full-wave and mode-matching solvers before machining, and corrugated and dual-mode horns feed most satellite earth-station dishes. Babinet’s idea returns in frequency-selective surfaces and metasurfaces, where a pattern of slots passes one band and the complementary pattern of patches reflects it. Search for standard gain horn, corrugated horn and slotted waveguide array.

figure.caption: The H-plane section of the optimum horn of the first worked example, to scale. The wave spreads from the apex, so its front is curved: at the edge of the 100 mm opening it lags the centre by δ ≈ 11 mm, 0.375λ, the most an optimum H-plane flare allows. A longer horn would be flatter; a shorter one would lose gain.
